Meaning (Layman Explanation): The formula used to decide the 'best split' (e.g., Gini, Entropy, or Log Loss for classification; MSE for regression).
Significance (Why It Matters): Determines how the model measures impurity — affects how splits are chosen.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): The maximum number of levels (layers) in the tree.
Significance (Why It Matters): Controls how complex the model can get. Limiting depth reduces overfitting.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): The minimum number of samples required to split a node into two branches.
Significance (Why It Matters): Prevents overfitting by avoiding splits on very small sample groups.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): The minimum number of samples required in a leaf node (final branch).
Significance (Why It Matters): Ensures leaves represent enough data — smoother predictions and better generalization.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): The number of features the model can consider when making a split.
Significance (Why It Matters): Introduces randomness and helps balance accuracy vs. speed. In Random Forest, promotes diversity among trees.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): Sets a limit on the number of leaf nodes in the tree.
Significance (Why It Matters): Simplifies the model and reduces overfitting by restricting structure size.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): The minimum drop in impurity required to make a split.
Significance (Why It Matters): Prevents unnecessary splits that don’t improve performance significantly.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): The strategy for choosing splits: 'best' (best possible) or 'random'.
Significance (Why It Matters): Affects tree randomness and speed — 'best' is accurate; 'random' adds slight randomness.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): Sets a seed for reproducibility of results.
Significance (Why It Matters): Ensures consistent output when you rerun experiments.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): The number of trees in the forest.
Significance (Why It Matters): More trees = more stable and accurate predictions, but slower training.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): Whether each tree uses a random subset of data (sampling with replacement).
Significance (Why It Matters): Increases diversity among trees → improves generalization and reduces overfitting.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): Number of CPU cores to use for training in parallel.
Significance (Why It Matters): Speeds up training, especially with many trees.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): Fraction or number of training samples used per tree.
Significance (Why It Matters): Helps control randomness and training speed — smaller samples add variety.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): Whether to use 'out-of-bag' samples (unused data) to evaluate model performance.
Significance (Why It Matters): Provides a built-in unbiased estimate of accuracy without a separate test set.

Meaning (Layman Explanation): Reuses previously fitted trees when adding new ones.
Significance (Why It Matters): Saves time if you’re experimenting with more trees iteratively.
